newsitem.title: FRANCE: Arafat says has US OK to negotiate pullback.
newsitem.headline: Arafat says has US OK to negotiate pullback.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was quoted on Friday as saying he had assurances from the United States and Europe that he would be able to negotiate the scope of future Israeli pullbacks from occupied areas.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has insisted he had a written U.S. guarantee that Israel alone would define the extent of three further withdrawals from West Bank areas due to follow the handover of most of Hebron this month.
Despite the U.S. State Department apparently confirming Netanyahu's view, Arafat told the French newspaper Le Monde:

"According to the accords, this (the withdawals) must be negotiated with us. It is expressedly mentioned in the Oslo-2 accord and also stated in letters of guarantee which we have obtained from the Americans and the Europeans," he said.

Le Monde, which interviewed Arafat in Gaza, said he did not divulge details of the letters. But the newspaper, quoting a "very good source", said there was no contradiction in the texts of the European and American letters he had received.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in a statement in Washington last week that Israel would define the extent of the planned witwhdrawals.
Under U.S. documents accompanying the Hebron deal, the other withdrawals agreed by Israel in a 1995 interim self-rule accord are due to start in March and be completed by mid-1998.
Arafat also challenged Netanyahu's contention that no documents barred Israel from continuing to build new settlements in occupied areas.
"That is false. If they build new settlements or enlarge existing ones, we will not stand by passively. The entire world will also not stand by if there is such a violation of the accords," he said.
Arafat expressed confidence that Washington would continue to apply pressure on Israel for new steps in the peace process "because President Clinton wants to go down in history".
Arafat denied he would have to make new changes to the Palestinian Charter which once called for Israel's destruction, saying those articles "which contradicted our peace accord have been cancelled.
"The Israelis want us to draft a new Charter when they don't even have a constitution. We'll have one when they have one," he said.

Arafat, who said he had "always been an optimist in the worst of situations", added: "I see the light at the end of the tunnel." Le Monde said Arafat added with a smile: "I can even get a glimpse of Jerusalem."
